Excellencies, ladies and gentlemen, if you could take a seat, please. We will start shortly. Very good. Excellencies, distinguished ministers, esteemed delegates and guests, good afternoon. My name is Megan Gilgen. I am the Director of Strategic Partnerships at UN Women, and it is my distinct honor to moderate this roundtable. Can I just say I am also extremely excited about the energy in the room. I think it bodes well for a very vibrant discussion. On behalf of UN Women and the Government of the Republic of Croatia, I'm delighted to welcome you to the G77 and Emerging Partners Ministerial Roundtable on Technology-Facilitated Violence Against Women and Girls. We will commence with remarks from His Excellency Mr. Andrej Plenkovic, the Prime Minister of the Republic of Croatia, followed by an opening address from Dr. Sima Bahous, Executive Director of UN Women. His Excellency, Mr. Gordon Gerlich Radman, Minister of Foreign and European Affairs of the Republic of Croatia. And we will also hear from Charlena Arapora, a survivor, advocate and founder of the Little Girl Project. Next, we will transition into our centerpiece segment, the high level ministerial dialogue featuring distinguished representatives from Turkey, Nigeria, Bangladesh, Croatia, and the Institute for Strategic Dialogue. We will conclude with an interactive dialogue bringing together government representatives, youth delegates, private sector leaders, and academia. I take this opportunity to express UN Women's sincere gratitude to the Republic of Croatia for co-hosting this critical and timely dialogue. We are exceptionally honored by the presence and leadership of Prime Minister of Croatia, His Excellency Mr. Andrej Plenkovic, today. Without further ado, it is my privilege to invite His Excellency the Prime Minister to deliver his opening remarks.

Thank you very much. Good afternoon. First of all, let me greet the distinguished Under-Secretary-General and the Executive Director of UN Women. Madam Seema Bahus, thank you, Minister Gerlich-Radman, for co-hosting this event. Madam Raputo, thank you for your presence. Madam President, Kolinda Grabar-Kitarovic, nice to see you again in the United Nations, where you feel like at home. I would like to use this opportunity, first of all, to address you. on behalf of the Croatian government and thank the entire team of the foreign ministry, of our ministry of justice, as well as the permanent representation here for close cooperation with the UN Women in many aspects and for many years. This has been a longstanding, fruitful cooperation from both sides. We know that Croatia is participating here in order to make a difference, in order to help and to respond. For us, gender equality and the protection of women and girls are core values guiding both our domestic policies and our international engagement. Croatia is one of few countries in the world that introduced femicide. as a standalone criminal offense in our national legislation. We promoted this step and our policies in relevant United Nations bodies, including through the Commission on the Status of Women. Commitment to gender equality and protection of women and girls is also readiness to respond to the challenges of our time, unfortunately. New and emerging technologies are rapidly transforming our societies. They have contributed to creating unprecedented and positive opportunities for women and girls. However, technology is also misused, even weaponized. Today, we gather here for an urgent challenge: technology-facilitated violence against women and girls. Online violence is not simply a digital problem. It causes profound and prolonged psychological, social, economic, and physical harm. Very often, what begins online does not remain online. Such criminal behavior is later often a fertile ground for new generations of offenders and, unfortunately, new generation of victims. Artificial intelligence is adding a new dimension to this challenge. Its rapid development offers enormous opportunities, including for bringing down criminals and offenders. But it can make abusive content easier to create, replicate, and disseminate at unprecedented speed and scale. Our response must therefore be equally ambitious. First, we need strong laws and effective enforcement. Technological innovation moves faster than our ability to protect fundamental rights. So we need to step up our cooperation. Second, we need greater accountability from technology companies and digital platforms. Innovation and freedom of expression must go hand in hand with responsibility. Appropriate policies accompanied by robust and adaptable systems are a must. Third, we need more data and research accompanied with stronger international cooperation. Technology-facilitated violence crosses borders by its very nature. No country can address it alone. At the same time, we need to establish better interaction with the industry. And fourth, we must invest in prevention and education. We need to equip young people with the knowledge and necessary values, including how to use technology responsibly. Finally, digital transformation must advance human rights, equality, and human dignity. The digital space should be a space in which every woman and every girl can participate freely, safely, and equally. It must remain a tool for empowerment, opportunity, and equality. Let us therefore use today's discussion to identify challenges and possible solutions and to strengthen our collective determination to act. Thank you very much for this opportunity.

Thank you very much, Your Excellency, for the opening remarks and for Croatia's continued leadership on this vital agenda. I am now pleased to give the floor to the Under-Secretary-General of the United Nations and Executive Director of UN Women, Dr. Sima Bahous.

Thank you, Excellencies, colleagues and partners, all protocols observed. I warmly thank the Republic of Croatia for co-hosting this ministerial roundtable with UN Women, and I also thank Prime Minister Plenkovic for bringing us together here today. I thank the G77 for its sustained support for gender equality in multilateral spaces. By taking up this issue during the General Assembly's high-level week, you are bringing the safety of women and girls online to the highest level of political discussion, and we thank you for that. I also thank Minister of Foreign and European Affairs, Gordan Grlic-Radman, for your support, Excellency, and allow me to also welcome Ms. Charlena Irupa, founder of The Little Girl project for raising awareness and for strengthening the protection of children. Digital technology, Excellencies, has opened new doors for women and girls. It connects them to education, to work, services, and public life. We want those doors to remain open and to open wider. Yet, many women and girls face threats and abuse when they step through them. Technology can be used to harass, survey, and silence. The harm can follow them offline into their homes, their work, and their communities. And we all lose when women are pushed out. We lose a journalist's reporting, a candidate's leadership, a girl's idea. This is happening on a scale we cannot ignore. Seven in 10 women surveyed by UN Women in the public sphere has faced online violence linked to their work. Four in 10 reported related harm offline. Our gender snapshot this year shows how often women are shut out of decisions that affect their lives. Digital spaces are now part of public life. we must remove the barriers that keep women from participating safely and from shaping the technologies of the future. Yesterday, the Secretary-General reminded the General Assembly of the promise of artificial intelligence and the need for accountability as it advances. That call speaks to our work here. Generative AI can create new opportunities It can also be used to fabricate intimate images, impersonate women, and spread disinformation. As technology advances, so must the protection of women and girls. We do have a shared commitment to build on. At the 67th session of the Commission on the Status of Women, Member States called for zero tolerance of violence carried out or amplified through technology. We agreed on the direction. Now, together, we can show what that commitment delivers: stronger prevention, protection for survivors, and greater accountability from those who build and govern digital spaces. Women's rights organizations helped put this issue on the international agenda. Their knowledge continues to lead us towards solutions. As technology changes the lives of women and girls, they need a strong voice for gender equality at every table where its future is being decided. If we do not do that, we will be embedding more inequality in the future of technology, actually in the current present of technology. This is the role of UN Women, and this is the role that UN Women was created to play. UN Women works with them, with member states, with technology partners to prevent abuse, to strengthen protection and access to justice, to improve the evidence and to support survivors. This roundtable is an important chance to bring those efforts together. Let us share what works. Let us make technology safer from the start. Let us invest in the women leading this work. Together, we can build a digital future in which every woman and every girl is free to participate, free to lead, free to thrive, and free to shape what comes next. I thank you.
Thank you, Executive Director. I now have the pleasure of giving the floor to the Minister of Foreign and European Affairs of Croatia, His Excellency Mr. Gordon Grlic-Radman. Thank you, Excellency.

Thank you so much, and Mr. Prime Minister. Distinguished Under-Secretary-General, Madam Sima Bahous, distinguished ministers, my dear colleagues here, and also the Shalena Erapuru, survivor, advocate, and founder, Little Bear Project. I welcome you. Dear colleagues, and of course, our Madam President, Kolinda Grabar-Kitarovic. Ladies and gentlemen, it's really my pleasure to welcome you to this ministerial roundtable, co-hosted by Croatia and UN Women. It was just a year when we also had a similar meeting here. That means Croatia is really ready to be a trustful partner on this. I am sure that so there will be also next year as well here. It's anger, as you mentioned, and it's a very important project and very important topic for ISAI dedicated to. This event is dedicated to a challenge that touches every society represented in this room, technology facilitated violence against women and girls. As Prime Minister of Croatia and Mr. Plenkovic said, digital technology has opened extraordinary opportunities for women and girls to learn, to connect, to lead, to be heard, and to be heard. Yet the same tools are increasingly being turned against them. Various online harmful practices are imposing damage on real lives globally. Millions of women and girls still lack legal protection from these harmful practices. These are not abstract figures. Behind every number is a woman silenced, a girl afraid to go online, a journalist, activist or leader pushed out of public life. Croatia takes this challenge seriously, both at home and on the international stage. Gender equality is enshrined in our Constitution, in our legislation and other strategic documents. The elimination of violence against women remains among our top priorities. In 2024, we amended our criminal code to explicitly define gender based violence. As also Prime Minister mentioned, as an aggravating circumstances and to introduce a criminal offense of femicide. Furthermore, our government criminalized the misuse of sexually explicit recordings, including their non-consensual distribution. Our newest act also set clear, coordinated procedures across police, justice, health, and social welfare systems. We also recognize that legislation alone is not enough. Prevention must begin as early as possible. Our schools now embed digital literacy, online safety, and respectful, non-stereotype relationship across curriculum. Also, National Media Literacy Portal equips children, parents, and teachers to recognize and respond to online violence. In addition to that, our welfare, and labor laws work together to ensure that no woman is left without protection or support, whether the violence she faces begins online or offline. One lesson stands out clearly. Technology-facilitated violence is not virtual. Its consequences are entirely real. They may escalate into physical violence. That is why our actions cannot be confined to a single government institution, a single sector or a single country. That require governments, technology companies, educators, justice system and civil society working together. This is precisely why Croatia gladly joins the UN Women in convening this roundtable. We hope that today's exchange will strengthen our collective political commitment, generate practical partnership, and help build digital spaces that are safe, inclusive, and rights-based for every woman and girl worldwide. Thank you so much, and I look forward to our discussion. Thank you very much.
Thank you, Your Excellency. And I now have the honor to introduce Ms. Sharlina Arapuro, survivor, advocate, and founder of the Little Girl Project.

Thank you so much all for being here. And thank you so much, UN Women and the Republic of Croatia, for giving me this immense honor. My name is Sharlina Arapuro, and I am an artist, survivor, and founder of Little Girl Project from Finland and Sweden. When I was being sexually abused as a child, I wrote speeches like this one to survive. I wrote about the things that I wanted to say and change. And when I wanted to die, I promised to stay alive so that I could be in rooms like this in front of people like you, telling you what needs to change. But unfortunately, I am not alone. I stand here today on behalf of every single woman and every single girl who might never have the privilege to speak in rooms like this, and every single survivor who have never received justice, and every single survivor who have not lived long enough to tell their story. I am speaking here on behalf of all of them on this global crisis. The global research estimates that every single second, 10 children are being sexually exploited and abused online. That is 300 million children every single year. This is not happening somewhere else. This is happening right here and right now on all of your cell phones and laptops right in front of you. And we need to stop treating online violence as though it has less harm, because it doesn't. Also, research tells us otherwise. A clear research has found that survivors from childhood sexual violence, which included an online element, reported more long-term and worse consequences than every category measured compared to survivors whose abuse did not have an online element. And it makes sense. I know it might be hard to comprehend because technology is new, but listen to me when I tell you that I understand that, not only as an advocate, but as a survivor. Because the abuse I survived did not end when the act itself ended. It just got worse. It followed me and it still follows me. It shattered my sense of self. It shattered my rights to my own body. And like I sing in my music, it stole pieces of me that belongs to me. Technology makes this abuse last forever and it never goes away. A few months ago, I sat in the European Parliament as a survivor, listening to a woman who lost her child to online sexual abuse. And that child could have been me. Luckily enough, I wrote these speeches. But when I was a child, shame convinced me that I somehow was alone and that it was my fault. Because even when I spoke and reported, I wasn't believed, helped, or supported. When we fail to make this a political priority, we are adding another layer to that silence and to that shame. We fail every single girl and woman out there with that silence, and we are all as a collective failing right now. Today, technology is creating new ways to silence women and girls every single second. They are being exploited and abused. And AI generated abuse does not make the harm artificial, although the technology might be. The violation is not. I did not come here just to tell you about what happened to me. I came here to ask what we are going to do next. Just like the Prime Minister said, we have to make this a political priority. We need clear and stronger laws. What is illegal and accepted offline must also be illegal online. It has the same consequences, if not even worse. AI generated child sexual abuse material and non consensual, non consented sexual deepfakes must be explicitly addressed and removed immediately because technology crosses borders like we just heard. Our response must also. Hold tech companies accountable. We can create safety by design, not when the harm has already happened. We need to prevent, detect, and remove this abuse. Governments, tech companies, and countries must work together because no single country can solve a problem alone that crosses all of these borders. We need to build justice with survivors and give survivors accessible long-term help and support. Because survivors' knowledge can be learned from things that doesn't even include in a policy paper. That's why it's such a great honor to speak here as a survivor on behalf of all the survivors. But do not ask what happened to us. Ask what would have protected us. Whilst I've been speaking here today, an estimate of over 3,000 children have been sexually abused online. Every one of them, a child just like I was, a childhood broken and a pieces of them stolen. We have survivors in every single country, in every single language, in every single community. This is not somebody else's crisis. It is all of ours together. So I hope you listen, but more importantly, I truly hope that you finally act. Because I was a little girl and I luckily stayed alive, hoping that I could be here in this room today to make a change. And today, I was lucky enough to keep that promise. But there are many who didn't. Thank you so much. Please act so that no other child and no other women has to make the same promises and the same speeches that I just did.

Thank you so much, Ms. Arapura, for those very impactful remarks. I think the executive director must leave to another engagement, but we very much thank you for being here. And we We look forward to commencing the panel discussion. I will first turn to Her Excellency Ms. Maniher Ozdemir Goktas, thank you, Minister of Family and Social Services of the Republic of Turkey. Turkey has taken important steps in recent years to recognize and address the growing risks that women and girls face in digital spaces. The inclusion of digitalization and artificial intelligence as a cross-cutting priority in the fifth National Action Plan on Combating Violence Against Women demonstrates a strong commitment to responding to these emerging challenges. As your ministry moves from policy commitments to implementation, what concrete measures are envisaged through the Fifth National Action Plan to prevent and respond to emerging forms of technology facilitated violence against women and girls while ensuring coordination with technology companies and public institutions? Your Excellency.

Honorable ministers, dear participants, it's an honor and privilege to address you today. Digital technologies are transforming our lives while expanding women's access to employment, education, the knowledge economy, and decision making. However, this technology can also enable new forms of violence against women and girls. Platforms that disregard their safety can become tools of discrimination and abuse. They are just online threats, harassment, stalking, intimate intimate image abuse and misuse of personal information are urgent global concern. AI generated fake images are also used to threaten and humiliate women and girls. We must take swift, decisive and effective action to prevent victims from being subjected to ongoing harm and threats. We need comprehensive action to prevent victims to protect victims, ensure access to justice, and empower women and girls. Technology companies must have clear responsibilities, sanctions for non-compliance, and effective complaint and response mechanisms. Safety and human rights must guide digital services, while our laws keep peace. Illegal content must be removed without delay. Perpetrators must face legal consequences, while victims need secure channels that protect privacy and provide rapid support. We must strengthen the judiciary, law enforcement, and social services to address technology-facilitated violence. Dear participants, in Turkey, we combat all forms of violence against women with zero tolerance, strong legislations, and updated policies. digitalization and artificial intelligence from a cross-cutting pillar of our 5th National Action Plan. The Turkish penal code criminalized the unlawful disclosure of private images or recordings and stalking with heavier penalties for sexual harassment through electronic means. Under our law 6284, we protect women regardless of the means used to commit violence. Our Violence Prevention and Monitoring Center support victims and use technology to strengthen protection. Since 28, women under threat have been able to use CADES. This is a mobile application to request help from the nearest law enforcement team with a single tap. We monitor high risk victims and perpetrators through electronic monitoring bracelets in cooperation with the Ministry of Interior. Turkish National Police has established a unit specifically dedicated to combating cybercrime. Our national action plan includes new guidelines on digital violence and rights protection, as well as digital safety and media workshop for women and children who are victims of violence. We are also developing a module to help young women and girls recognize and respond to digital violence. dear guests, stronger digital literacy and awareness are essential for women, girls, children, families, educators and professionals. Digital violence knows no borders. We must try and on international cooperation, international standards, and we must share good practices and cooperate with all relevant stakeholders. Turkey stands ready to expand. international cooperation and share its experience so that together we can build a safer and more equal digital future for all women and girls. I thank you.

Thank you, Excellency, for outlining the actions taken by your government. I now raise a question to Her Excellency, Ms. Hajja Iman Suleiman Ibrahim, the Minister of Women's Affairs of the Federal Republic of Nigeria. Nigeria has taken important steps to strengthen violence against its response to violence against women and girls, including through the Violence Against Persons Prohibition Act and the Cybersecurity Act, providing legal foundations to address forms of abuse that also occur in digital spaces. Excellency, as Nigeria strengthens its response to technology facilitated violence against women and girls, what lessons have emerged from applying existing cybercrime and gender based violence frameworks? And what are the government's priorities for ensuring effective prevention, survivor centered support and accountability in digital spaces?

Thank you very much, moderator. May I start by extending courtesies to the Prime Minister who is here and the ED of the UN Women. I would like to thank the Government of Croatia and the UN Women for this convening. I would like to recognize my colleagues, Turkey, Bangladesh and other countries that are present. I would also like to recognize the survivors. Without survivors, we will not know how better to do stuff. And I hope that we'll leave this room with better reasons to be able to collaborate and do more around cyber crimes on our women and girls. Nigerians experiences have established a fundamental principle that the digital space may be new, but the violence is not. Technology has changed the tools used to perpetuate abuse on our women and girls. It has not diminished the state's responsibility to protect the women and girls. Technology also has further reinforced the need for government, the private sector, the tech companies, also the NGOs and civil societies and communities to work together in ensuring that we address this critical challenge that we face. Accordingly, the ongoing review of our Nigerian Violence Against Persons Prohibition Act of 2015, the Child Rights Act of 2003 is of critical importance to us. This effort is to ensure that our protection framework reflects contemporary realities, including cyberstalking, online harassment, impersonation, sextortion, image-based abuse, and the online exploitation of our children. This review closes legal gaps. It defines offenses and jurisdiction clearly and more strongly. It establishes duties of service providers It will help to strengthen remedies and deliver a framework that fits the future that we see. However, legislations alone will not protect our citizens. Government must fund and coordinate a national system for prevention, early warning reporting, survivor center services, institutional coordination, effective investigation, and accountability. Our ministries, departments, and agencies will continue to publish clear mandates, designate focal points, and establish time-bound referral pathways, maintain secure case management systems, and report measurable results. Our law enforcement and justice institutions continue to investigate complaints promptly, preserve digital evidence, protect survivors from retaliation, and prosecute offenders in accordance with the law. Ladies and gentlemen, in Nigeria, we continue to strengthen the capacity of frontline institutions to identify, to investigate, and to respond to technology-facilitated gender-based violence. We also continue to strengthen and expand our social workforce so our survivors are able to access psychosocial support, legal, medical, and referral support promptly, confidentially, and without re-traumatization in the process. Recent responses to technology-facilitated abuse of our children have demonstrated the urgent need for a whole-of-government, whole-of-system approach, and whole-of-society approach that speaks to rapid coordination amongst women affairs authorities, our law enforcement agencies, our child protection actors, and all other relevant institutions. These bodies must designate responsible officers, active joint response protocols, and share information lawfully and securely, and conduct risk assessment and place the safety and dignity of survivors at the center of every response. Prevention must begin before the first click, not after the first crime. Government and development partners have continued to finance nationwide digital safety education, require age-appropriate safeguards in schools and public services, and support accessible reporting channels. The private sector, the tech companies, must take ownership and full responsibility and rise to the occasion in addressing this critical challenge that we face as a people. Institutions must train the teachers, health workers, social workers, and community leaders to recognize warning signs, document incidents safely, and refer survivors without delay. Speed and safety should penetrate at the same level and get the same attention. Communities must challenge victims blaming. They must support survivors, protect children's privacy, and report abuse through trusted channels. Technology platforms must meet their responsibilities by applying safety by design, strengthening accessibility reporting, and rapid takedown mechanisms, notifying users about risk and decisions. preserving evidence for lawful investigation, and disrupting repeat offenders, and cooperating fully with competent authorities while protecting users' rights and privacy. Ultimately, what is violence offline does not cease to be violence because it occurs online. Women and children are entitled to the same dignity, safety, justice, and support in the digital space as it is in the physical world. Government must continue to set and enforce standards, fund services, and hold perpetrators and neglect actors accountable. Institutions must operationalize those standards through trained personnel, coordinated procedures, and transparent monitoring. Technology platforms must prevent abuse, respond quickly to reports, and provide lawful access to evidence, and communities must promote safe, digital behavior, support survivors and report harms. We must also, for Nigeria, just like the rest of the world, the task to regulate technology is not simple, but it's urgent and is very, very important. We'll continue to ensure that our laws, our institutions, our social protection systems evolve as rapidly as the technologies used to perpetrate these harms. Strengthen clear implementation plans, dedicate resources Regular public reporting, independent oversight, and sustained engagement with our survivors, civil society and communities, and the tech companies. This is the direction of our current reforms, and all responsible actors must contribute to delivering it. Nigeria stands ready to continue to collaborate with our sister countries to ensure that we have a strong response to this challenge. Thank you so much.

Thank you so much, Excellency, particularly for your emphasis on coordinated systems that connect protection, survivor support, justice, and frontline responders, and for your call that prevention must begin before the first click. I now turn to Her Excellency, Ms. Shama Obeid, Minister of State for Foreign Affairs of Bangladesh. Bangladesh has brought strong national attention to digital violence against women and girls, including through the Ministry of Women and Children Affairs leadership in convening a national dialogue under the 16 days of activism. Minister, building on Bangladesh's national dialogue and its commitment to stronger laws, coordinated institutional responses and public awareness, What are the government's priorities for moving from recognition of digital violence to a survivor centered, multi-sectoral response? Thank you.

Excellencies, ladies and gentlemen, I truly thank Croatia and UN Women for convening this so important roundtable today. Violence against women takes many forms, while many cases remain under-recognized and unreported. We must therefore continually strengthen policies and practices to protect women and girls from both persistent and emerging threats. Technology-facilitated violence is one such threat. Women and girls are increasingly targeted through digital harassment as AI tools are used to harass, defame, impersonate, and endanger them online. Mr. Chair, Bangladesh has a strong legacy of addressing violence against women. Our first female prime minister, Begum Khaleda Zia, advanced policies promoting women's participation across all spheres of life and strengthening their protection. Building on this legacy, the present government under Prime Minister Tariq Rahman is strengthening legal and institutional responses, including coordinated action for faster investigation and trials of violence against women and girls, alongside stronger accountability and deterrence. A dedicated women only pink bus service has also been launched recently with female drivers and conductors to provide safer public support on the streets. In addition, we have strengthened coordination on legal and social protection, rehabilitation, safe shelter, psychological support and skills development for women and girls. We are we all review our national cybersecurity laws, but I truly believe that laws are not enough. We believe that a consolidated, a collaborated global effort is needed to combat this situation. When we listen to strong voices like Ms. Arapora, we know that we need to do more. Our response also addresses emerging digital threats. We recently convened the Dhaka Dialogue to develop voluntary guidelines for states on preventing, investigating, and remedying digital harassment against women and girls. We will establish a Friends of the Dialogue and a technical working group to develop a reference document on definitions and standards. I, to say not the least, I would like to talk about our peacekeepers who continue to support peace and recovery in post-conflict settings. And a lot of them are also women, where the risk of sexual violence remains acute. Our peacebuilders support justice, reform, and women's participation in peace processes. furthermore providing shelter to Rohingya women and girls reflect our commit commitment to protecting women afflicted by conflict and persecution. We invite all the member states to partner with Bangladesh in the initiative of of preventing this digital harassment against women and children for all. Thank you.

Thank you so much, Excellency. As we move to the European space, across Europe, there is a growing attention being paid to the rise of online harassment, cyberstalking, image-based abuse, and other forms of technology-facilitated violence. We know that Croatia has recently strengthened its broader legal framework on violence against women, including through reforms to criminal legislation. while also participating in national and European discussions on digital violence and efforts to align with the EU Directive on Combating Violence Against Women and Domestic Violence. I would now invite State Secretary, His Excellency Ivan Cernich. Your portfolio sits at the intersection of justice and digital transformation. From your experience, how can governments leverage digital innovation to improve reporting, survivor support, and access to remedies for women and girls experiencing online abuse?

Thank you for the great question. Yes, indeed, I do believe that my ministry is very interesting, very unique within European Union, and I assume, I guess, also broader, because this combination of justice and digital transformation is definitely, I would say, the justice system has a lot of benefits from it. To answer maybe your question in a way, you know, digitalization and means that we are now investing into digitalizing our judicial system is also helping, I think, in the context of our specific today's subject. Because simply, you know, we have in Croatia one system which is called e-communication. which is allowing communication of not only institutions, but also parties within judicial proceedings with the courts online. And this is definitely increasing the efficiency of the whole judicial process. So here for the victims of violence against women and domestic violence and sexual violence, this is definitely beneficial because simply the justice will be rendered faster. Yes, you mentioned some of the things that we have recently done. Prime Minister and Minister have also been mentioning our separate specific criminal offense of femicide, which we have introduced two and a half years ago, which makes us also quite unique because we are just one of four out of in total 27 European Union member states which has this kind of crime offense. And it is defined as a gender-based murder of a woman. So killing a woman simply because she is a woman. We have here imposed the harshest sanctions there are in Croatia. And also there is no statute of limitation. Regarding the criminal offense of abuse of sexually explicit content, or sexual explicit recordings. This has been done more than five years ago. So I think we were kind of pioneering there also. And it is, of course, the perpetrator here is misusing the relationship of trust by simply, you know, using this sexual explicit recording, which was made for personal use and making it available to the third party. And so it's basically what we know as revenge ****. And also within this criminal offense, we have a deep fake ***********. So when you are misusing someone's image again and replacing it with someone else's image. And also we have as a, as a co-qualificatory elements for this offense, if it has been made available to the larger number of persons. And then, of course, typically through social networks. And then, of course, the sanctions are much harsher, much stricter. We also have a security measure of a ban on use of internet, or a ban on internet access. And that is happening, of course, when the criminal offense is being conducted online and there is a risk that it can be repeated. So we have done a lot and we are still doing a lot. You have mentioned the EU directive. We are right now transposing directive and it includes some, let's say, new offenses, but most of them we already do have within our criminal legislation. So the revenge **** the cyberstalking, cyber harassment, cyber incitement to hatred or violence. Also interesting, right to be forgotten, the victim's right for the erasure of the sexually explicit content. We have all this, but still, by transposing the directive, we do believe that we will achieve even a greater level of protecting of women against violence. And one other thing that I also wanted to mention and conclude with it is also that, in fact, last week we had a proposal by the European Commission of the EU Kids Act. And this is something what Charlena was talking about, what we do believe that we will have assurance, we will have greater responsibility for online services. And of course, as some of the previous speakers have mentioned, legislation is not enough. Implementation is crucial. Also, technology is not enough. I would say that digital literacy is essential here. So I would simply concluded by saying that protecting children requires a combination of effective regulation, responsible technology, and informed families. Thank you.

Thank you, Mr. Sernich. And I think all of our speakers on the panel speaking for government are showing the demonstrable progress, but also some of the challenges that remain. I would now have the pleasure of introducing Ms. Sasha Hevlechic, founder and CEO of the Institute for Strategic Dialogue, who is the last speaker for this panel. We know that there is growing awareness of the so-called manosphere ecosystem that radicalizes young men and boys into worldviews that normalize and exacerbate violence against women and girls. What does your analysis tell us about the current landscape of threats that are facing women and girls online? And drawing on your extensive experience working with policymakers, regulators, and civil society, what are the most effective solutions to counter the growing influence of online misogyny?

Thank you so much. moderator, thank you for your partnership, for your leadership. Indeed, thank you to all of the countries sitting around the table highlighting this unbelievably important issue. My organization has been working to detect and analyze all forms of online hate, abuse, extremism. And we know this, of course, sitting around this table. Ask any girl, ask any woman in public life. The scale and extent of online harassment, abuse, violence has gone through the roof with the rise, of course, of digital technologies. And now we have a whole new set of challenges that present themselves with generative AI. We have worked together with UN Women, with Equimundo on some research, as you've pointed out, of the manosphere, where we've seen the combination of certain subcultures online and the algorithmic processes and capabilities of social media amplify mainstream certain cultures that were hitherto really stuck in the fringes where they needed to stay. The algorithmic system will take you from something completely innocuous, and often this is for minors, this is boys, not men, will take you into an environment that normalizes rape, that normalizes gender-based violence and abuse, the kinds of things you wouldn't believe are being served to children. So I think that we have, in many ways, heard everything that we need to hear from Ms. Arapuru. Thank you so much. You are so brave. We really should just follow your lead on this. Distinguished colleagues, the violence against women and girls stands in the face of humanity as the most widespread and systemic human rights violation globally. Its magnitude is unparalleled. an estimated 736 million, which is approximately one in three women, have been subjected to physical and/or sexual violence. It is grounded in deeply rooted structural inequalities, reinforced by discriminatory social norms and power imbalances. Nowadays, it goes even beyond. The technology-facilitated violence is an emerging phenomenon that often goes unrecognized and unreported, while its prevalence remains of the highest concern. Let us be clear, the online violence does not exist in isolation from offline violence. It is part of the same continuum. What happens online can have serious consequences for women's physical and psychological well-being, economic opportunities, and participation in public life. Montenegro, therefore, strongly supports addressing technology-facilitated violence through a human rights-based, survivor-centered, and intersectional approach. Effective action requires strong and enforceable legal and regulatory frameworks. Legislation should keep pace with technological developments and provide effective protection and remedies. Responses should be coordinated across borders, as technology-facilitated violence does not stop at national boundaries. The technology sector has a particular responsibility. This is particularly important in the development and deployment of artificial intelligence, where existing gender biases can be reproduced or amplified at scale. Finally, accountability must go hand in hand with prevention and survivor support. Civil society organizations, women's rights organizations, and relevant regulators play a critical role and should be adequately supported. Montenegro remains committed to work with all partners to ensure that digital transformation advances rather than undermines gender equality and the full enjoyment of human rights by all women and girls. Thank you.
